one_liner: Rust-to-WASM Filecoin CommP (piece commitment) hasher; 11-34x the throughput of @web3-storage/data-segment in Node and browsers.
what_it_does: Computes the Filecoin piece commitment (FR32 padding, SHA-256 truncated to 254 bits, binary Merkle tree padded with zero commitments) for a byte stream. The npm package @hugomrdias/commp-wasm exposes root(data), digest(data) and a streaming create() hasher with write/digest/count/reset/free; digest() returns the same PieceDigest fields (code 0x1011, padding, height, root, multihash bytes) as data-segment's multihash hasher, so it is close to a drop-in for that module. The WASM binary (about 22 KB) is inlined as base64 and instantiated synchronously, so there is no async init.
how_it_is_fast: All three steps (FR32 pad, leaf hashing, tree reduction) run inside one WASM call per 1 MiB chunk instead of one JS-level SHA-256 call plus fresh Uint8Array allocations per 64-byte node, which is how data-segment works. Leaves are batched 128 quads (256 leaves) at a time and hashed with a hand-written 4-lane SIMD128 SHA-256 (one message per u32 lane of a v128, transposed in and out), and the second compression block uses a precomputed K+W table because every message is exactly 64 bytes. Completed subtrees go onto an O(log n) binary-counter stack and zero-padding commitments are computed once and cached.
when_to_use: Computing CommP / piece CIDs for Filecoin or Storacha uploads in a browser, Deno, Bun or Node where native addons are unwanted.
Large uploads streamed in chunks: memory stays O(log n) (about 3 MiB RSS growth for a 1 GiB payload in the repo's M1 Pro run).
Replacing @web3-storage/data-segment's multihash hasher when hashing is the bottleneck; same digest layout, checked against data-segment and Lotus vectors.
Bundler-free setups: inline base64 WASM needs no .wasm asset handling or async init.
when_not_to_use: Server-side bulk CommP where native code is allowed: the project's own native Rust build is 681 MiB/s single-threaded and 3,738 MiB/s with the parallel feature on an M1 Pro, versus 183 MiB/s for WASM; go-fil-commp-hashhash reaches 728 MiB/s (derived ratios 3.7x and 4x from page data). The native crate is not published on crates.io.
You need piece aggregation, inclusion proofs or segment indexes: this only hashes; data-segment's aggregate/proof APIs have no counterpart here.
Payloads above 127 * 2^47 bytes (MAX_PAYLOAD_SIZE): write() throws RangeError.

Maturity-sensitive deployments: npm package created 2026-09-30, 0 stars, single author; issues #2-#7 fixed off-by-one height, wrong empty-input padding, a usize overflow above about 31.75 MiB and a destructive build() in the week before the benchmarks.

integration.dependencies: none at runtime (inline WASM; Rust build uses wasm-bindgen, sha2 0.11 and talc)
integration.min_toolchain: Node >= 24 per repo engines; WASM SIMD128 support in the engine; rebuilding needs Rust 1.92.0 (pinned in compare/), wasm-pack and binaryen wasm-opt
integration.platforms: any JS engine with WebAssembly SIMD (Node, Chromium, Firefox, WebKit, Deno, Bun per README)
integration.thread_safety: Single-threaded WASM instance; one hasher per stream, not documented for workers sharing an instance
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same PieceDigest fields and multihash bytes as data-segment's multihash hasher, but a separate package with its own create(); hashers should be freed with free() (a FinalizationRegistry frees them eventually)

gotchas: Harness note: in Node the baseline's SHA-256 is node:crypto createHash per 64-byte node (sync-multihash-sha2 node export, native and hardware SHA-capable), wrapped in new Uint8Array, Digest objects and spread pushes; in browsers it is @noble/hashes (pure JS). So the 11.8 MiB/s Node baseline (about 85 ms per MiB, roughly 33,000 hash calls, about 2.6 us per call, derived) measures per-call and allocation overhead, not SHA arithmetic; the speedup comes from fusing and batching, not from a faster compression function.
The README's 'Fast JS (@webbuf/sha256)' row is not pure JavaScript: commp-js's own header says it uses WASM-backed SHA-256.

The bench hashes one constant 1 MiB buffer (fill(4)) per iteration with create/write/digest/free; no implementation has a data-dependent shortcut, so this does not inflate the numbers, but it is a single size and the WASM row includes the copy into WASM memory.
WASM memory never shrinks; the JS wrapper feeds writes in 1 MiB chunks to bound it. Forgetting free() leaves cleanup to the FinalizationRegistry.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: hash-wasm, fast-noble-hashes and awasm-noble give faster generic SHA-256/BLAKE3 to JS, but a CommP built on them still pays one JS-to-WASM call per 64-byte node (the README's @webbuf row reaches only 41 MiB/s that way); pick commp-wasm when the output you need is the Filecoin piece commitment itself.
verified_claims_summary: First-party tinybench run (100 ms / 250 iterations, one 1 MiB buffer, create-write-digest per iteration) on Apple Silicon, probably the M1 Pro of compare/results: WASM 181.2 MiB/s vs data-segment 5.3.x 11.8 MiB/s in Node 26 (15.4x); in browsers 185.6 vs 7.5 (Chromium 153), 170.7 vs 5.0 (Firefox 155), 187.3 vs 16.5 (WebKit). The separate compare/ run (M1 Pro, Node v26.10.0, 1 GiB) reproduces the WASM rate at 182.8 MiB/s and shows native Rust and Go faster.
status_note: Active (last commit 2026-10-01, all 11 issues closed) but two weeks old with 0 stars; MIT per README and npm (crate says MIT OR Apache-2.0, no LICENSE file), small and dependency-free enough to vendor.
